title: Interleaving String
description:
Given strings `s1`, `s2` and `s3`, decide whether `s3` can be formed by **interleaving** `s1` and `s2`: split both `s1` and `s2` into pieces, then alternate pieces from each so that the characters of `s1` stay in their original order and so do the characters of `s2`.

Return `true` if such an interleaving exists, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: aa | dbb | c | bca | c alternates pieces of s1 and s2.

hints: If the lengths do not add up, the answer is immediately false.
Think of walking through s3. At each step the next character came from either s1 or s2. The state you need is how many characters of each you have consumed so far.

dp[i][j] = can the first i+j characters of s3 be formed from s1[:i] and s2[:j]. It is true if (dp[i-1][j] and s1[i-1] == s3[i+j-1]) or (dp[i][j-1] and s2[j-1] == s3[i+j-1]). One row of length len(s2)+1 suffices.
signature: def isInterleave(self, s1: str, s2: str, s3: str) -> bool:
approach:
**Key insight: the only thing that matters about a partial interleaving is how many characters of `s1` and of `s2` have been used. Those two counters also determine the position in `s3`.**

Let `dp[i][j]` be true when `s3[:i+j]` is an interleaving of `s1[:i]` and `s2[:j]`. The last character `s3[i+j-1]` came from one of the two strings:

`dp[i][j] = (dp[i-1][j] and s1[i-1] == s3[i+j-1]) or (dp[i][j-1] and s2[j-1] == s3[i+j-1])`

with `dp[0][0] = true`. The answer is `dp[m][n]`, after an early exit when `m + n != len(s3)`.

**Why it is correct:** any interleaving of the prefixes ends with a character from `s1` or from `s2`, and removing it leaves an interleaving of shorter prefixes. The recurrence considers both cases exhaustively, so no valid interleaving is missed and no invalid one is accepted.

**Space optimisation:** `dp[i][j]` depends only on `dp[i-1][j]` (same column, previous row) and `dp[i][j-1]` (already computed in this row), so a single row of length `n+1` updated in place is enough: before overwriting, `dp[j]` still holds the value from the previous row.

**Common mistakes:** greedy matching (when both strings offer the same next character you must try both); forgetting the length check, which breaks the index arithmetic; treating the problem as checking that `s1` and `s2` are both subsequences of `s3`, which is necessary but not sufficient.

**Interview follow-ups:** (1) Return one actual interleaving (keep parent choices and walk back). (2) Count the number of distinct interleavings (replace `or` with `+`). (3) Three input strings: the state becomes `(i, j, k)` and the table 3-D.
